title: Only about a quarter of my multiplayer game is what players actually see. Here is where the rest goes.
author: Curious_Ad5417
selftext:
Most AI game posts I see here are about looks. Models, textures, painted scenes. Fair, that is the part people notice first.

I counted where the work in my game actually sits, by share of the source code:

\- Automated tests: 34 %

\- Interface and layout: 27 %

\- Translations (5 languages): 17 %

\- Game logic (combat, economy, progression): 11 %

\- Balance data (beasts, buildings, curves): 8 %

\- Server and database rules: 4 %

So players see roughly a quarter. The rest is the boring part that keeps a multiplayer game honest.

A few things that live in that hidden part:

\- The server recalculates every fight with its own copy of the game logic. If the phone and the server disagree, the server wins.

\- The raid boss health is written into the database rules a second time. If the two ever drift apart, the server rejects honest hits, so a test compares them before every release.

\- When the cheat check finds something, it reports and locks. It never edits a save on its own.

\- Test accounts can never pay out real rewards. Every payout has its own check for that.

And one honest failure, I planned our first world boss against a simulation instead of real player numbers. On the first evening the players took 21 % of its health. Since then every boss and event gets checked against real data first.

The tests are the biggest single block on purpose. With AI writing a lot of the code, they are how I know a change did what I asked and nothing else.

How it's made, code with Claude Code, art from AI image tools and Blender, every system and every number decided and tested by me.

Curious how this looks for others here, how much of your project is stuff nobody will ever see?
